name: Peripheral Nerve Injuries and Limb Deformities

reference.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students / Hoppenfeld's Physical Examination
clinicalPearls: Radial nerve injury at spiral groove of humerus causes wrist drop with sensory loss over first dorsal web space; triceps is spared
Ulnar paradox: higher ulnar lesion at elbow causes LESS clawing than a low lesion at wrist because FDP to digits 4-5 is denervated
Carpal tunnel syndrome: compression of median nerve under flexor retinaculum; thenar wasting, ape hand, numbness of lateral 3.5 digits
Common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds around fibular neck; injury paralyses dorsiflexors and everters, producing foot drop and high-stepping gait
Seddon classification: neuropraxia (conduction block, axon intact), axonotmesis (axonal severance, sheath intact), neurotmesis (complete transection)
reference.pathophysiology: Nerve trauma produces Wallerian degeneration distal to the injury site within twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Axons regenerate at approximately one millimeter per day from the proximal stump. Prolonged denervation beyond twelve to eighteen months results in irreversible motor end-plate atrophy and fibrous replacement of muscle fibers.
additionalDifferentials: Cubital tunnel syndrome vs Guyon canal compression
Common fibular nerve entrapment vs L5 radiculopathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) performed 3-4 weeks post-injury
High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound for nerve continuity or neuroma
